rounds.intro:
**Round 1: the big decisions.** Each answer here fixes the shape of one or more specs. Later rounds go into detail only where needed.

- For each question, **form your own view first**. *Claude's take* is collapsed for that reason.
- Pick an option, or choose *Other*. Put any nuance in the notes: a half-answer with a good note beats a clean but wrong choice.
- If a question is badly framed, or you want to talk it through, use **Flag for discussion**. Flagged questions count as answered, and I'll pick them up in chat.
- Sketches: the *domain model*, *disk format* and *context budget* questions each have an interactive illustration.

Save when you like, as often as you like. Then tell me **next**.

**Round 2: reconcile, then detail.** Round 1 is folded in: every round-1 card now shows a *Settled* summary. Check that the summaries say what you meant.

Three kinds of question this time:

- **Reconcile**: places where your answers pull in two directions (tree vs merge vs cross-links; regenerate on the board vs in your notes).
- **New threads** from your notes: spaces, provenance, tone, mid-session model choice, editing, merge, the spawn animation.
- **Default checklists**: a list of small behaviours I'd write into the spec. **Tick each one you accept**; anything left unticked gets reopened in round 3, so write why in the notes.

After this round most specs can move from *draft* to *review*.

**Round 3: confirm, then review.** Round 2 is folded in. All decisions so far are collected in one digest, [`DECISIONS.md`](DECISIONS.md) in this folder, which the spec writers work from.

This round is short:

- **Confirmations** of things I inferred or proposed from your notes (navigation, links, text selection, spawn numbers, storage details).
- **The review gate**: tick each spec you approve as-is. Specs appear in the Specs tab as they are written, and the remaining nine are being drafted now. Anything you don't tick, tell me what's wrong in the notes.

When every spec is ticked, the specs step is done and I write the v0.1.0 plan.

**Added after the specs were drafted:** six more questions (*click to light*, *sign-in*, *delete*, *subject menu*, *defaults*, *smaller proposals*). These are decisions the spec writers needed and had to propose; nothing goes into a spec as agreed until you tick it.

**Specs step closed (2026-10-02).** All 13 specs are agreed and marked *stable* in the wiki; the v0.1.0 implementation plan is `agent_wiki/plans/v0-1-0.md` (Specs tab). No questions this round. This workshop stays available: a spec change during implementation goes through a new round here, so the reasoning stays on record.

**Round 5: the Choose room.** Lantern gets its second room, **Choose** (name picked in chat on 2026-10-12 over *Buy*, *Weigh* and *Seek*): it helps you choose and buy something you know nothing about yet (your example: a 3D printer).

Already decided in chat (2026-10-12) and recorded in the wiki: Welcome and Gallery belong to each room; no Home page for now (maybe later); the app opens on the room you were in. Think, Explore and Interview are in the backlog as the rooms after Choose.

This round has two parts:

- **Frame** (5 questions): what changes in the app so it can hold more than one room. Today the code still assumes Learn in a few places (the shell, the Gallery stats in Rust, the settings, and the node kinds and states in the core model).
- **Choose room** (11 questions): what the room is for, how a session goes, what is in the graph, and where facts like prices come from.

As before, my take is collapsed: answer first. Anything you are not sure about, flag it to discuss.

**Round 6: Choose room details.** Round 5 is folded in: the new spec **Choose room** is in the Specs tab (draft), and the frame changes are amendments marked *round 5* in Rooms and spaces, Domain model, Product scope, Settings and Subject storage.

This round settles what round 5 left open: the graph space's name, where the decision board lives, the subject status, what the web is used for and which sources count, Compare, the recommendation, tone, the room's settings, the file format, and one contradiction between two of your answers (*Open in Learn*).

When this round is answered the Choose room spec can go to review, then I write the v0.2.0 plan (frame release first).

**Round 7: Choose, ready for code (v0.2.0 B2).** All six Choose designs are accepted and recorded. The new spec **Choose protocol** (Specs tab, draft) writes down what the room stores, what the model is told and must answer (with the source rules in its system prompt), what each call receives, and the evals.

Most of it follows from your earlier answers. These questions are the points I had to invent. When they are answered, the protocol and Choose room specs go to review, and B3 (the provider's web tools) can start.

**Round 8: the companion.** The little lantern of the identity (release v0.2: six finite gestures, no behaviour yet) comes into the app. The new spec **Companion** (Specs tab, draft) already holds your four opening notes as rules:

- **CO-1** It can be turned off in Settings, and then it shows up nowhere.
- **CO-2** No feature depends on it: whatever it gives access to (a chat, for example) keeps its own entry point and keeps working without it.
- **CO-3** On Welcome, interacting with it gives tips, predefined, not generated.
- **CO-4** Anywhere, it can be the guide to using the app; that is where its role starts.

These questions turn that into behaviour: where it sits, what a click does, what *guide* means first, the gestures, calm in Study, hiding, colour and idle. One sketch shows four placements in the three spaces.

**Round 9: Amber.** Your round 8 answers are in the **Companion** spec (Specs tab): the name, hanging from the header with a rope you can grab, the resting positions, tips, the guide, Ask Amber on Haiku 5.5, the gestures and the rules. RS-33 is amended as you accepted.

Your notes added a lot, and a few of them pull against boxes you ticked. The first four questions put each conflict side by side; the rest fill in the new features. The last question sorts everything into a first version and later.

questions.title: What is still off in the PoC?
questions.context:
You judged the PoC *very close* (2026-09-29), but the roadmap lists **what is still off** as the first input to the specs, and none of it has been written down yet.

List anything that felt wrong, missing, slow, confusing or annoying, with the worst first. Rough is fine, for example: *"lighting a node takes too long"*, *"I wanted to add my own question as a node"*, *"too much text per node"*. Each item becomes a requirement or a recorded non-goal.
questions.take:
Things I would expect from reading the code. Check whether you felt them:

- **~25 s per light-up**, and the new nodes only appear at the very end of the stream.
- **Exactly 3 options, always**. There's no way to dismiss one, ask for others, or add your own.
- **Tree only**. Two related concepts on different branches can't be linked.
- No way to **edit, delete or regenerate** a node, and no **cancel** while it streams.
- *I get it* marks a node understood with no trace that it was self-declared rather than shown.
- The home screen is minimal: you can't rename subjects or see progress.

settled.summary: Recorded as requirements across product-scope, domain-model and the round 2 questions: provenance and token counts on nodes, resizable panel, dismiss/more/own options, edit and correct content, delete, regenerate (see q-r2-regenerate), cancel, a welcoming home, model choice mid-session, a settings panel with room submenus, real prompt engineering and context management, Ctrl+click merge. Latency is **not** a constraint; it is masked by animation. New concept: **rooms have spaces**.

questions.title: What must not change?
questions.context: The other side of the same question: what felt **right** and must survive the rewrite? Naming it protects it. A rewrite tends to lose the details nobody wrote down: the travelling light, the tone of the tutor, the 3-teaser rhythm, the stats line…
questions.take: From the record, at least: the learning-node design (r008-02 *Forward embers*, final); the *never dump everything, exactly-3-teasers* method; streaming text into the panel; and saving as you go with no Save button. I'll treat these as kept unless you say otherwise.

settled.summary: Kept: palette, subtle motion and travelling light, the calm *warm light in a peaceful place* feel (other rooms may get their own lantern, but the app stays coherent), the 3-teaser rhythm, secondary but accessible stats, a **mandatory legend**, the header elements, and a right-hand reading panel with markdown. Tutor tone becomes selectable (q-r2-tone). *Text highlight* is clarified in q-r2-highlight.

questions.title: What is v0.1.0 for?
questions.context: This one decision sets the quality bar: installer or not, onboarding or not, how much error handling, how much the data format has to last.

options.label: Your daily tool
options.detail: A Learn room you use for real, every day. Built and run from source, or a local installer. Polished where you feel it, rough where only a stranger would notice.

options.label: A shareable release
options.detail: Others can install it from GitHub and get going without you: installer, first-run onboarding, a README for users, CLI login checks.

options.label: A foundation
options.detail: The Learn room plus the room framework (room definitions, room switching), so Think can follow quickly. Less polish on Learn itself.

questions.take: **Your daily tool**, with one firm constraint: the **data model and on-disk format are designed for several rooms** from the start, even though only Learn ships. Your subjects then survive v0.2, and we don't pay for a room framework before a second room exists to test it. A foundation built for one room usually ends up designed around that one room anyway.

settled.summary: **Your daily tool**, designed modular from the start: multiple rooms (not all about learning) and new mechanisms must be addable without a rewrite. Reusable components are a requirement.

questions.title: Which rooms ship in v0.1.0?
questions.context: Only Learn exists (PoC). Think has a seed (the *make me think* / socratic skill). Explore, Decide and Discover are names only.

options.label: Learn only
options.detail: Harden the PoC loop into a real product. Rooms appear only in the data model.

options.label: Learn + Think
options.detail: Two rooms prove the room abstraction is real: different AI role, different node vocabulary, same subject.

options.label: Learn + Think + a room switcher
options.detail: Two rooms plus taking one subject from one room to the other.

questions.take: **Learn only.** The PoC proved Learn is worth building; nothing yet proves Think's graph vocabulary (positions, objections, replies). Specifying Think properly would double this spec round. Lock the format so Think fits, and make Think the headline of v0.2.

settled.summary: **Learn only.** Rooms are present in the model and the UI frame, but there is no second room.

questions.take:
My placement for *your daily tool, Learn only*:

- **v0.1.0**: library, cross-links, add my own node, dismiss, more options, edit/delete, cancel, scalable context, model setting, search, rich content (math and diagrams), installer, keyboard navigation.
- **Later**: regenerate, parallel generation, API provider, local provider, export, undo/history, spaced review, learner profile, bring your own material, Think, auto-update, light theme, French UI.
- **Never**: nothing yet. *Never* is for things that would betray the idea, such as a plain chat mode with no graph.

The most debatable calls are **parallel generation** (a big win for the 25 s waits, but it complicates sessions and saving) and **undo** (cheap if storage is designed for it from day one, expensive to add later).

settled.summary: **v0.1.0:** library, cross-links, add my own node, dismiss, more options, edit/delete, cancel, scalable context, model setting, math & diagrams, installer, keyboard navigation. **Later:** regenerate (reopened in q-r2-regenerate), parallel generation, API/local providers, search, export, undo, spaced review, learner profile, own material, Think, auto-update, light theme, French UI. **Never:** nothing.

questions.title: How do rooms relate to a subject's graph?
questions.context: The README says a subject **visits** rooms and that a room sets *what nodes and edges mean*. That leaves open whether each visit grows its own graph, or whether all rooms share one graph. Even with only Learn in v0.1.0, the format has to commit to one or the other. Open the sketch to compare the two.

options.label: A: one graph per room visit
options.detail: learn/ and think/ each hold their own nodes and edges. A concept that matters in both rooms exists twice, possibly linked.

options.label: B: one shared graph, rooms add layers
options.detail: One set of nodes per subject; each room adds its own state, nodes and turns on top.

options.label: Decide in v0.2
options.detail: Store v0.1.0 data under a learn/ room folder and choose when Think is designed. Risk: a migration later.

questions.take: **A.** It matches the *room furnishes the space* metaphor: Learn's *understood* and Think's *objection* are different kinds of things, not states of the same node. It's also the only option that's simple now. A *same concept as…* link across rooms can come later without breaking anything. B looks elegant, but it forces every room to agree on what a node is, and that agreement is exactly what we don't know yet.

settled.summary: **A: one graph per room visit.**

questions.title: Tree, or graph?
questions.context: The PoC is a strict **tree** (`parentId`). That gives one path to every node, which is what makes breadcrumbs, the route highlight and the tree layout work. Real knowledge has cross-links: *Fast retransmit* relates to *Slow start* on another branch.

options.label: Tree only
options.detail: Keep the PoC shape. Relations are mentioned in text only.

options.label: Tree spine + cross-links
options.detail: Every node keeps exactly one parent (the path you discovered it by). Extra **typed edges** (relates, prerequisite…) are drawn differently and don't change the path.

options.label: Free graph
options.detail: No privileged parent; any node can have several. Breadcrumbs and tree layout need rethinking.

questions.take: **Tree spine + cross-links.** The spine keeps everything the final learning-node design relies on (route highlight, travelling light, tree layout). Cross-links add what the tree can't say. Who creates them comes next round: the tutor through a tagged block, you by hand, or both.

settled.summary: You chose *tree only*, but asked for **merging (two parents)** and **relations written in the text**, rebuildable by any parser. The board also places cross-links in v0.1.0. The proposed reconciliation is in q-r2-shape.

questions.title: Which node states beyond open → lit → understood?
questions.context: Today: **open** (proposed, dark), **lit** (explained), **understood** (shown or declared). Select every addition you want. Selecting none keeps the PoC states.

options.label: Dismissed
options.detail: A proposed node you won't pursue. Hidden or faded, but kept so the tutor doesn't propose it again.

options.label: Shaky
options.detail: Lit, and you tried, but a check showed a misconception. A natural place to come back to.

options.label: Self-declared vs demonstrated
options.detail: Not a new state but a flag on *understood*: did you pass a check, or press *I get it*?

options.label: Mastery level
options.detail: A 0–3 scale instead of a single *understood*.

questions.take: **Dismissed** plus the **self-declared/demonstrated flag**. Both are cheap and both carry real information: the tutor stops re-proposing dismissed nodes, and the graph is honest about how sure you are. *Shaky* is attractive but needs the tutor to judge misconceptions reliably. That's better tested after v0.1.0.

settled.summary: States: **open → lit → understood**, plus **dismissed**. *Understood* records **how**: demonstrated or self-declared.

questions.title: Who decides that a node is understood?
questions.context: In the PoC the tutor can emit `<understood/>` after a good answer, and you can toggle *I get it / Not sure anymore* yourself.

options.label: The tutor only
options.detail: Understood means you passed a check. No self-declaration.

options.label: Both, as in the PoC
options.detail: Either way, and no record of which.

options.label: Both, recorded
options.detail: Either way, but the node records *demonstrated* or *self-declared* and shows the difference (for example a solid fill vs an outlined check).

questions.take: **Both, recorded.** You stay in charge (sometimes you just know it), and the graph stays truthful. The visual difference has to fit the final node design. I'd keep the solid amber fill for demonstrated and propose a variant for self-declared in the UI round.

settled.summary: **Both, recorded.** The tutor (after a check) or you can mark a node understood, and the node records which one did.

questions.title: How many next steps does the tutor propose?
questions.context: The *exactly 3, genuinely distinct* rule comes from the learning-session skill. It gives the graph its rhythm, but it can force a third option that isn't worth much, or leave out a good fourth.

options.label: Always exactly 3
options.detail: Keep the rule as it is.

options.label: 3, and you can ask for more
options.detail: Always 3; a *More options* action asks for 3 different ones.

options.label: The tutor decides, 2 to 5
options.detail: Fewer on narrow topics, more on broad ones.

questions.take: **3, and you can ask for more.** The rhythm is part of the product's feel and the method's discipline. *More* removes the frustration without losing that discipline.

settled.summary: **3, and you can ask for more.**

questions.title: What context goes to the model on each turn?
questions.context: Today the whole map is sent as an outline on every call. That's fine at 40 nodes, but grows without limit. Play with the sketch: node count, explanation length, dialogue turns. It shows the three strategies' token totals and what each one hides from the tutor.

options.label: Whole map
options.detail: Keep the PoC strategy; revisit when it hurts.

options.label: Neighbourhood
options.detail: Path, siblings, children, the parent's explanation, plus the **titles** of every other node (so no duplicate proposals), and the last N dialogue turns.

options.label: Neighbourhood + memory
options.detail: As above, plus short stored summaries of lit nodes and a learner profile. Needs extra LLM calls to write the summaries.

options.label: Adaptive
options.detail: Whole map while it fits a budget, then switch to the neighbourhood. Same results as the PoC for small subjects.

questions.take: **Adaptive.** Small subjects (most of them, for a while) keep the PoC behaviour you liked. Big ones degrade gracefully instead of failing. *Memory* needs summary-writing calls, and with ~3 s of overhead per CLI call that's a real cost. It belongs with the latency work, after v0.1.0.

settled.summary: **Adaptive**: the whole map while it fits a budget, then the neighbourhood plus the titles of every node.

questions.title: Which latency levers for v0.1.0?
questions.context: Measured: ~3 s of fixed overhead per `claude -p` call, ~12 s for an introduction, ~25 s to light a node. Streaming hides part of it, but the new nodes only arrive at the end.

options.label: Options first
options.detail: The tutor writes the options block *before* the explanation, so the new nodes appear within seconds. Changes the tagged-blocks protocol.

options.label: Cheaper model for cheap tasks
options.detail: Suggestions, check questions and short replies go to a faster model (Haiku/Sonnet); light-ups to the main one.

options.label: Long-lived CLI session
options.detail: One CLI process kept alive and fed by stdin (stream-json input), removing the ~3 s spawn cost. Needs a spike to confirm the CLI supports it cleanly.

options.label: Prefetch
options.detail: Quietly light up likely next nodes in the background. Costs tokens, may waste them.

options.label: Accept it
options.detail: Streaming is enough for v0.1.0.

questions.take: **Options first** and **cheaper model for cheap tasks**. Both are prompt- or config-level changes with a big perceived gain. The long-lived session is the real fix, but it's an unknown: I'd put a time-boxed spike into the v0.1.0 plan rather than promise it in the spec.

settled.summary: **Accept the latency for v0.1.0**, and mask it with motion: while a node lights up, child nodes grow out of it as neutral shapes until their titles arrive (q-r2-spawn). Options-first and a cheaper model for cheap tasks come in a later version.

questions.title: How does a subject live on disk?
questions.context: The README asks for *readable and diffable, possibly an OKF bundle, so the prism tooling can read it*. The sketch shows the same subject stored three ways, with the git diff of one node becoming understood in each.

options.label: A: one JSON file
options.detail: The PoC format, extended with rooms and edges. Simplest; opaque in diffs; one atomic write.

options.label: B: folder, JSON graph + markdown bodies
options.detail: graph.json holds the structure (one atomic write); each node's explanation and dialogue is a markdown file.

options.label: C: an OKF bundle
options.detail: One markdown file per node with YAML frontmatter (kind, state, parent, links). Prism opens it as a wiki. Structure is spread across files.

questions.take: **C, the OKF bundle**, because it serves a goal you named: your subjects become first-class knowledge that Prism, git and any markdown reader can use, and the format outlives Lantern. The costs are real but bounded. Lantern needs a frontmatter parser, and a multi-file change (deleting a subtree) isn't atomic, so the spec must define write order and recovery. Loading 500 small files is milliseconds. If interoperability matters less to you than I think, **B** is the safe pragmatic choice.

settled.summary: **One JSON file per subject**, now and probably for good. Export formats (an OKF bundle, for example) are a later feature.

questions.title: Where do subjects live?
questions.context: PoC: `Documents/Lantern/subjects/<id>.json`.

options.label: Documents/Lantern
options.detail: Fixed, as in the PoC.

options.label: A library folder you choose
options.detail: Default Documents/Lantern, changeable in settings. Point it at a synced folder or a git repo.

options.label: Several libraries
options.detail: Open any folder as a library, like a vault in Obsidian.

questions.take: **A library folder you choose**: the default works with no setup, and pointing it at a git repo is what makes a diffable format pay off. Several libraries can come later without a format change.

settled.summary: **A library folder you choose**, defaulting to Documents/Lantern.

questions.title: What happens to subjects made with the PoC?
questions.context: PoC subjects are `lantern-poc/1` JSON files. You may have some you care about.

options.label: Import them
options.detail: v0.1.0 converts PoC files on first launch and keeps the originals.

options.label: Drop them
options.detail: The PoC was throwaway; so is its data.

questions.take: **Import them.** It costs about a day, and keeping your first real subjects builds trust in the tool.

settled.summary: **Import** `lantern-poc/1` subjects, keeping the originals.

questions.title: Graph and panel: keep the PoC layout?
questions.context: PoC: graph on the left, panel fixed at 44% on the right, header bar with room chip, title and stats.

options.label: Keep it
options.detail: It works.

options.label: Keep it, made adjustable
options.detail: Resizable split; collapse either side (graph full screen to look at the map, panel full width to read).

options.label: Rethink it
options.detail: For example the panel as an overlay over the graph, or a reading mode. Becomes an agent_design component.

questions.take: **Keep it, made adjustable.** You validated the layout. Resizing and collapsing are cheap and cover both *survey the map* and *read deeply*. A real rethink belongs in the design workflow, not in the specs.

settled.summary: **Keep it, made adjustable**: resizable split, and either side collapsible.

questions.title: Interface language?
questions.context: The tutor already answers in the subject's language. This is about the app's own buttons and labels.

options.label: English
options.detail: Single language, no i18n layer.

options.label: French
options.detail: Single language.

options.label: English + French
options.detail: An i18n layer from day one.

questions.take: **English** for v0.1.0, with all strings in one module so French can be added cheaply later.

settled.summary: **English.** All UI strings live in one module; French comes later.

questions.title: Platforms?
questions.context: Prism ships Windows only. Tauri can build macOS and Linux, but each one needs testing, and the CLI provider's process handling differs (for example `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` on Windows).

options.label: Windows only
options.detail: Like Prism.

questions.take: **Windows only**, with no Windows-only assumptions outside the provider and paths modules, so a port stays cheap.

settled.summary: **Windows only.**

questions.title: What quality bar?
questions.context: The PoC has one ignored Rust test. Pick what v0.1.0 must have.

options.label: Unit tests for the core
options.detail: Protocol parsing, graph mutations, storage round-trip, context building.

options.label: Rust tests
options.detail: Provider stream parsing (with recorded CLI output), file I/O, path safety.

options.label: UI end-to-end tests
options.detail: Playwright against the web build with the fake tutor: the main loop works.

options.label: Prompt evals
options.detail: A small fixed set of subjects run against the real model, checking protocol adherence (3 options, valid JSON, language). Run by hand, not in CI.

options.label: CI
options.detail: GitHub Actions running everything except the evals on each push.

questions.take: The first four. The **prompt evals** matter most: the tagged-blocks protocol is the product's spine, and a prompt change that quietly breaks it would be invisible to every other test. Add CI if the repo goes public.

settled.summary: Core unit tests, Rust tests, UI end-to-end tests with the fake tutor, and prompt evals. **Evals run on a cheap model (Haiku)**: if Haiku follows the protocol, larger models will too, and the same harness can later qualify local or custom providers. No CI.

questions.title: In your own words: when is v0.1.0 done?
questions.context: One or two sentences, or a short list of scenarios that must work. This becomes the acceptance section of the v0.1.0 plan, and specs get trimmed against it.
questions.take: A draft to react to: *I can start a subject, learn it over several days across app restarts, and the graph shows honestly what I know, with no data loss, no waits over ~10 s before something useful appears, and no need to open a terminal.*

settled.summary: *I can start a subject, learn it over several days across app restarts, and the graph shows honestly what I know, with no data loss. Waits over ~10 s are fine because the animation carries them, there's no need to open a terminal, and at least a minimal settings panel lets me customise the app.*

questions.title: Rooms and spaces: where do Welcome and Gallery live?
questions.context:
From your notes: *each room can have multiple spaces*. For Learn: a **learning space** (the PoC graph + panel), a **welcome** space (start a new subject or continue one of the 3 most recent), and a **gallery** to browse past explorations with their stats.

This mirrors Prism's *project → lens → view*: a room owns its set of spaces, the way a lens owns its views. The open point is whether Welcome and Gallery belong to **each room** or to **the app**.

options.label: Per room
options.detail: Each room has its own welcome, gallery and working space(s). Learn's gallery shows Learn progress (understood %); a future Think gallery would show its own measures. The app opens on the **last used room's welcome**.

options.label: App-level welcome and gallery, per-room working spaces
options.detail: One welcome and one gallery for all rooms, listing subjects with every room they visited. Rooms only provide their working space.

options.label: Both
options.detail: An app-level welcome (pick a room, see recent work in any room) plus per-room spaces.

questions.take: **Per room**, because what a gallery should show (what *progress* means) is a room's business, exactly like a Prism lens owning its views. With one room, an app-level home would be an empty layer. When the second room arrives, a room switcher in the header (beside the room name) is enough, and an app-level home can be added then without changing any room. Please also give the three spaces names in the notes if *Welcome / Study / Gallery* doesn't fit.

settled.summary: **Per room.** Learn owns Welcome, Study and Gallery. The app opens on the last used room's Welcome.

questions.title: Reconcile: tree, merge, cross-links, relations in text
questions.context: Round 1 pulled in three directions: **tree only** (the q-model-shape choice), **merge nodes with two or more parents** (your notes and Ctrl+click), and **cross-links in v0.1.0** (scope board), with a wish to keep **relations in the text** so another parser could rebuild the graph.

options.label: Parents + links in text
options.detail: A node has `parents[]`: none for the root, 1 normally, 2 or more for a merge. That's the only structural edge. **Relations live in the text**: explanations and dialogue can link to other nodes (`[Slow start](node:n2)`, written by the tutor or by you). They're clickable in the panel and can be drawn as faint lines in the graph (toggle). No separate edge list, so the file is the text plus parents.

options.label: Parents + typed edge list
options.detail: As A, plus an explicit `edges[]` (relates, prerequisite, contrasts) created by the tutor through a tagged block or by you.

options.label: Parents only
options.detail: Merge yes; relations stay plain prose. Cross-links move to Later.

questions.take: **Parents + links in text.** It honours all three wishes. The spine stays a tree except at merges, so the route highlight and travelling light keep working; a merge node's route lights all its parent paths. Merges are first-class. Relations are in the prose, where they mean something and any markdown parser can recover them. A typed edge list can still be derived from the links later. The tutor protocol gains one rule: *link to existing nodes by id when you mention them.*

settled.summary: **Merge is Later.** v0.1.0 is a tree, with relations as links in the text (confirm in q-r3-links).
